catalog_quote: (5) Summary of metrical parameters a. The final syllable is extrametrical, unless extrametricality would render the whole word invisible or unaccentable. b. Northern East Cree is quantity-sensitive at the level of the nucleus. A heavy (H) syllable contains an historically long vowel or a rising diphthong. A light (L) syllable contains an historically short vowel. c. There is no Weight-By-Position. d. Feet are iambic; footing is from the right edge of the word, excluding the final syllable. e. There are no degenerate (L) feet. f. End Rule Right: the rightmost metrical prominence is accented. ... (6) Extrametrical final syllable a. The final syllable is never accented. b. Either the penult or antepenult is accented. (5b): Evidence for quantity-sensitivity is provided in (7): Northern East Cree accents the penult if it is heavy; otherwise it accents the antepenult. ... new_statements.quote: Le déplacement de l'accent relève de l'apophonie suprasegmentale et consiste, pour ce qui est de l'iyiyiw, en un déplacement de l'accent, provoqué par le suffixe -ih4 [scanned: -//z4], vers la pénultième. Examinons le cas du marquage du pluriel inanimé nonimal [sic] : SINGULIER PLURIEL 38. a. /uta:pa:n/ → [u'da:ba:n] /uta:pa:nih/ [scanned: uta:pa:mh] → [uda:'ba:nh] « sa voiture » « ses voitures » b. /wi:pit/ → ['wi:bit] /wi:pitih/ → [wi:'bith] « sa dent » « ses dents » (p. 76) — Fn. 126, p. 399: Il y a déplacement de l'accent sur la dernière syllable : /ka:-mi'sa:c/ « cela est grand, gros » (II, SG) vs /ka:-misa:c-ih/ [ga:misa:'tʃ] « ceux-ci sont grands, gros » (II, PL)
new_statements.translation: Accent shift belongs to suprasegmental apophony and consists, for Iyiyiw, in a shift of the accent, triggered by the suffix -ih (position 4), to the penult. Consider the marking of the inanimate nominal plural: SINGULAR / PLURAL 38. a. /uta:pa:n/ → [u'da:ba:n] 'his/her car' / /uta:pa:nih/ → [uda:'ba:nh] 'his/her cars'; b. /wi:pit/ → ['wi:bit] 'his/her tooth' / /wi:pitih/ → [wi:'bith] 'his/her teeth' (p. 76). Fn. 126, p. 399: There is a shift of the accent onto the last syllable: /ka:-mi'sa:c/ 'it is big' (II, SG) vs /ka:-misa:c-ih/ [ga:misa:'tʃ] 'these are big' (II, PL).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Dyck, Brittain & MacKenzie 2006 account (one word accent, weight-sensitive; /-h/ plural shifts accent to the final syllable) and with the on-disk Rose & Brittain 2011 and Davies 2020, which say the same. Collette adds no weight statement and no general rule; he adds Whapmagoostui-dialect data on the -ih accent shift and on the accent domain (prefixes unaccented, preverbs independently accented). Quote is from the repository's extracted text layer: letter-spacing artifacts normalized, two scanned-garbled tokens flagged in brackets; original PDF not opened (too large).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No general placement rule is stated. Accent is treated only as a morphological exponent: the inanimate-plural / obviative suffix -ih (often inaudible, its vowel apocopated) moves the word accent one syllable rightward, which Collette calls 'to the penult' of the underlying form (p. 76, p. 273) and 'onto the last syllable' of the surface form (fn. 126, p. 399). His singular examples show accent on a long penult ([u'da:ba:n], ['wi:bit]). He also states that preverbs carry their own accent and prefixes carry none (p. 136), i.e. the accent domain is the word minus person prefixes. Short lax vowels are described as 'non accentuées' and subject to deletion (p. 42).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions. Fn. 126 gives a singular conjunct form with accent already on the final syllable (/ka:-mi'sa:c/), which the catalog's penult/antepenult non-final pattern would not predict; Collette does not comment on it. Preverbs (e.g. cî ABL., mâkwâ-, mistâ-) are separate accentual words; the perfective prefix cî- is discussed as a word bearing its own accent per James 1991 (fn., p. 146).
new_statements.identity_note: Collette 2014 describes the Whapmagoostui (Great Whale River) variety of the Northern dialect of East Cree (iyiyiw), based on his own fieldwork; he notes reported phonological differences between the Whapmagoostui and Chisasibi speech (p. 58 area, §3.1.2) and that some authors treat Whapmagoostui as closer to Naskapi. The catalog's source (Dyck, Brittain & MacKenzie 2006) and the on-disk companions (Rose & Brittain 2011, Davies 2020) are Chisasibi-based (CCLAS). Both are Northern East Cree = nort1552; no identity problem, but the dialect difference should be noted.

readall_conflicts: No substantive disagreement. Collette 2014 labels the same -ih-triggered shift 'vers la pénultième' (p. 76, p. 273) and 'sur la dernière syllable' (fn. 126, p. 399); the two labels refer to the underlying form (with the -ih vowel counted) and the surface form (vowel apocopated) respectively, and the surface reading matches the catalog source and the on-disk Rose & Brittain 2011 / Davies 2020, which describe the /+h/ morpheme as moving accent to the final syllable. One small unexplained detail: Collette's fn. 126 singular /ka:-mi'sa:c/ already has final accent in the singular, which the catalog's non-final penult/antepenult pattern does not predict; Collette gives no rule that would account for it. Collette states no general placement rule and no weight condition, so he neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's weight-sensitivity.

sources.quote: 'Each word in NE Cree contains one accented syllable, which correlates with a higher pitch, and to a lesser degree, intensity ... in the non-final accent pattern, words are accented on either the penultimate syllable or the antepenultimate syllable. When the penultimate syllable is long, accent falls on the penultimate syllable. When the antepenultimate vowel is long, and the penultimate vowel is short, accent falls on the long antepenultimate syllable. When both antepenultimate and penultimate vowels are short, the accent can fall on either syllable (MacKenzie 1980).' Final accent pattern wit

sources.quote: 'Syncope only affects syllables containing a short vowel (MacKenzie 1980) ... the location of syncope is predictable from foot structure; however foot structure is largely abstract, since there is only one pitch-accented vowel per word and hence only one "audible" foot (Dyck et al. 2006, 2008).' Confirms the single-accent domain and no secondary stress; silent on placement details.

sources.quote: 'NE Cree words have one pitch accent per citation form. Accent falls on one of the last three syllables ... The final accent is morphologically conditioned [suffix -h voids final extrametricality] ... Non-final accent either falls on the penult or the antepenult ... the penult is accented when it is long; in contrast, the antepenult is accented when it is long and the penult is short. ... if both the penult and antepenult are short, the rules of accent placement are unclear ... accent in some words might be lexicalized ...
